intro: Today marks a collision of eras: Anthropic just pulled off the largest IPO in history at $81.3 billion while Grand Theft Auto VI — built by 5,000 humans over 13 years without a single generative AI tool — launched to record-shattering reviews and nearly $4 billion in day-one sales. Meanwhile, the cracks in AI's breakneck expansion are showing, from 42 state attorneys general fighting to keep millions of users' private chats off the auction block in Character.AI's bankruptcy, to S&P eyeing a credit downgrade for Nvidia amid the Jensen Huang leadership turmoil. It's a lot — grab your coffee and let's get into it.

stories.title: 42 state AGs fight to block Character.AI's auction of users' private chats
stories.summary: A bipartisan coalition of 42 state attorneys general is trying to block Character.AI from auctioning over 21 million users' chat histories, including 2.1 million minors' accounts, during its Chapter 11 bankruptcy. The leading bidder was incorporated just days before being selected, with no disclosed parent company. The AGs argue the sale lacks safeguards: no requirement to honor existing privacy policies, no user data deletion mechanism, and no limits on further resale.
stories.opinion: The mystery bidder detail makes this increasingly suspicious — a shell company formed the day before selection, bidding on intimate conversations of millions of minors, with no transparency requirements. This may become a landmark case for data rights in bankruptcy. Where coverage differs: TechCrunch reports the shell company was 'formed one day before being selected'; The Verge says it was 'only incorporated on November 13, 2026'

stories.title: Anthropic's record $81.3B IPO coincides with GTA VI launch, the last monument to pre-AI game development
stories.summary: On November 26, 2026, Anthropic's $81.3 billion IPO — the largest ever — coincided with the launch of Grand Theft Auto VI, which earned $3.79 billion on release day and became the highest-rated game on Metacritic. GTA VI was made entirely without generative AI by roughly 5,000 people over 13 years, with 30,000 unique handcrafted NPCs. The piece frames GTA VI as likely the last game of its kind, a monument to human craftsmanship at the dawn of the AI efficiency era.
stories.opinion: A striking symbolic coincidence. The juxtaposition powerfully illustrates the tension between efficiency-driven AI and painstaking human artistry — and raises the question of whether audiences will eventually notice or care about the difference.

stories.title: S&P considers Nvidia credit downgrade over governance and 'key man' risks after Huang turmoil
stories.summary: S&P Global Ratings is considering downgrading Nvidia's credit rating from AA to AA- due to governance concerns following CEO Jensen Huang's ouster and reinstatement. The agency cites weak executive oversight, lack of succession planning, and heavy reliance on Huang. A decision is expected within 90 days. A downgrade could increase borrowing costs for Nvidia and for neoclouds and infrastructure companies whose debt Nvidia backstops, as Nvidia has arranged $500 billion in AI infrastructure financing where lenders were already pushing for larger guarantees.
stories.opinion: The ripple effects matter more than the one-notch downgrade itself — Nvidia's $500B in infrastructure financing means its credit rating is load-bearing for the entire AI buildout supply chain.

stories.title: OpenAI merges Chat and Work into a single ChatGPT interface with shared usage limits
stories.summary: OpenAI is merging its Chat and Work experiences in ChatGPT into a unified interface with a shared usage meter, rolling out first to Pro subscribers with broader availability in December. The company acknowledges its heaviest users may hit limits sooner, though Instant model conversations remain unlimited. Some subscribers are concerned the merger reduces access to advanced reasoning models. The move mirrors Anthropic's merger of Claude chat and Cowork interfaces in September.
stories.opinion: Framing a consolidation that may reduce power users' effective access as a UX improvement is a bold choice. The subscriber backlash will be worth watching, especially since the pricing hasn't changed.

stories.title: The Rundown's Thanksgiving AI cheat sheet covers Huang saga, hacking surge, and math breakthroughs
stories.summary: The Rundown's Thanksgiving edition provides a conversational guide to recent AI developments: Nvidia/Jensen Huang's temporary departure and return (adding $1T in stock value) amid Alice Huang spy allegations and Megaspeed chip diversion concerns; a surge in hacking as AI finds software bugs faster than they can be patched; major AI math breakthroughs including Anthropic's claimed Riemann Hypothesis solution and OpenAI's Navier-Stokes solution; a DIY system using AI vision to auto-mute TV ads during live sports for ~5 cents per game; and Stripe Atlas data showing 42% of new startups are building AI.
stories.opinion: A useful snapshot of how AI stories are filtering into mainstream dinner-table conversation. The breadth of topics — from trillion-dollar stock swings to a 5-cent ad-muter — captures how unevenly AI is landing across society.

stories.title: Google patent describes system for generating personalized AI video feeds and ads
stories.summary: Google filed a patent for 'My Channel,' a system that would generate personalized AI video feeds and advertisements using demographic data, viewing history, IP addresses, GPS locations, age, and contextual signals. The system would use LLMs to create prompts and generate tailored AI videos — including entire movies — on Google's servers. The patent has been rejected but Google could appeal or resubmit. It was filed in May 2025 and published last week.
stories.opinion: Even as a rejected patent, it's a revealing look at where Google's product thinking is headed — fully synthetic, hyper-personalized content streams that blur the line between entertainment and advertising in ways that make today's algorithmic feeds look quaint.

stories.title: Backblaze reveals it has been sharing customer data with advertisers since December 2025
stories.summary: Backblaze's new privacy policy, effective December 1, 2026, reveals the company has been collecting and sharing customer personal information — including identifiers, commercial information, geolocation, and internet activity — with advertising and marketing partners since December 2025. Backblaze told Ars Technica the policy's table format reads more broadly than intended and that disclosures relate to website and marketing cookies, not customer backup files. The company says its legal team will review the table for clarity.
stories.opinion: A cloud backup company quietly sharing customer data with advertisers for a year before updating its privacy policy is exactly the kind of trust erosion that drives customers to competitors — especially in a category where trust is the entire product.

tweet_headlines.headline: Inco AI's Splash 1.7.3 pushes Inkling 2 Mini's __context window to 261K tokens__ on a 36GB M5 Max, up from 101K, with vision support and 79 tps on coding prompts.
tweet_headlines.source_text:
🍎 A 24GB Mac is running Inkling 2 Mini with 👀 vision, 160K context, and up to 79 tps on coding prompts.

And on another Mac, someone pushed a conversation from 101K to 261K tokens before running out of memory.

Inco AI released Splash 1.7.3, bringing new local inference optimizations for Thinking Machines Lab's Inkling 2 Mini.

On a 24GB M6 Mac ...

🔥 Coding decode → up to 79 tps
👁️ Vision support → Images + text
🧠 Vision-enabled context → 160K tokens
💻 Local inference with GGUF + MLX
☁️ No cloud required

On a separate 36GB M5 Max system, the developer tested a long-running Inkling 2 Mini conversation.

Before the update:
🔴 Memory exhausted at 101K tokens
After Splash 1.7.3:
🟢 Conversation reached 261K tokens

The release also includes ...
✅ New Inkling 2 Mini vision support
✅ Improved memory management
✅ MLX checkpoint-loading fixes
✅ Support for additional quantized builds
✅ Better handling of long-running conversations

Long conversations and large codebases can consume enormous amounts of memory, especially when you want to keep everything local.

Getting more usable context and multimodal capabilities out of the same unified memory is a big deal.

Now we're squeezing substantially more context out of the same hardware (along with tokens).
